Chapter 5: The Limits of Justice and the Power of Memory
As the years rolled on and the final trials at the ICTY came to an end, people started asking—what could justice really accomplish after such overwhelming tragedy? For some, the tribunal’s verdicts brought relief. They felt reassured, knowing the world hadn’t forgotten what happened in Kosovo. For others, though, these decisions just highlighted how much was still left unresolved.
The truth is, international justice has its limits. From the very beginning, it was clear the tribunal could only put a few of those responsible on trial. That meant many who played a part in these crimes never faced a courtroom. And the process itself? It was slow—sometimes taking years to reach a verdict. Survivors waited, often in agony, and when the outcomes finally came, they didn’t always bring the closure people had hoped for. No sentence, no matter how symbolic, could erase the pain or undo the harm that had already been done.
But here’s where memory stepped in with its own kind of strength. Documenting what really happened—listening to survivors, collecting evidence, sharing these stories with the world—became an act of resistance. It pushed back against those who wanted to downplay or outright deny the crimes. For survivors, having their stories acknowledged was a way to feel seen, a reminder that their suffering was real and that their voices mattered.
In Kosovo, coming to terms with the past wasn’t easy. Whole communities remained divided, with old wounds still fresh. The shadow of violence lingered in daily life, shaping the way people related to each other and even how they saw their own futures. Some found comfort in remembering—through memorials, ceremonies, or simply by telling their stories out loud. Others struggled, stuck between wanting justice and the need to move forward and rebuild.
Despite its flaws, the tribunal did something important: it created a record that couldn’t just be swept away. That record became a foundation for future generations—a way for them to understand what happened and why. It wasn’t perfect, and it wasn’t complete, but it was a start. It stood as a reminder that, at least for a moment, the world was watching and cared enough to act.
For everyone involved—investigators, prosecutors, survivors—the experience left a mark that would never fade. Many walked away changed, their idea of justice shaped by hard realities. They discovered that holding people accountable is never simple, and that the truth is often up for debate. But they also learned something else: bearing witness, just telling the truth about what happened, can be its own kind of justice.
At its heart, the story of Kosovo isn’t just about violence or loss. It’s also about resilience—the determination to face the past and try to build something better. The tribunal and those who supported its work played a small but meaningful part in that larger struggle. Even when the odds felt impossible, their efforts proved that searching for truth and justice is always worth it.
